title: Component Composition and the Children Prop

subChunks.title: Component Composition and the Children Prop
subChunks.hookHtml: The most powerful thing in React isn't a single hook — it's the ability to compose components. You build small, focused pieces and assemble them into complex UIs. The children prop is the mechanism that makes wrapper and layout components possible: your component renders whatever you put between its tags.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Composition over configuration

Beginner React code often has huge components with a dozen props controlling every aspect of their appearance. Expert React code composes small components together:

// ❌ Configuraton-heavy — one component that does everything:
<Card
  title="Quest Log"
  subtitle="3 quests"
  icon="scroll"
  footerText="Last updated today"
  hasFooter={true}
  headerVariant="dark"
/>

// ✅ Composition — small pieces assembled by the caller:
<Card>
  <CardHeader>
    <ScrollIcon />
    <h2>Quest Log</h2>
  </CardHeader>
  <CardBody>3 quests</CardBody>
  <CardFooter>Last updated today</CardFooter>
</Card>

The children prop

Any JSX nested between a component's tags becomes the children prop:

function Card({ children }) {
  return (
    <div className="card">
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

// The h2 and p become Card's children:
<Card>
  <h2>Quest Log</h2>
  <p>Three quests completed today.</p>
</Card>

The component renders whatever its children are — it doesn't know what they are. This is the open/closed principle in React: closed to modification, open to extension via composition.

Layout components with children

function PageLayout({ children }) {
  return (
    <div className="page">
      <header className="top-bar">Arcane Academy</header>
      <main className="content">
        {children}
      </main>
      <footer className="footer">© 2025</footer>
    </main>
  );
}

// Every page gets the header and footer automatically:
<PageLayout>
  <QuestsPage />
</PageLayout>

Multiple slot pattern — named children via props

When you need more than one "slot", use additional props:

function SplitLayout({ left, right }) {
  return (
    <div className="split">
      <aside>{left}</aside>
      <main>{right}</main>
    </div>
  );
}

// Usage:
<SplitLayout
  left={<Sidebar />}
  right={<Content />}
/>

Forwarding children for flexible wrappers

function Button({ children, onClick, variant = 'primary' }) {
  return (
    <button
      onClick={onClick}
      className={`btn btn-${variant}`}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

// Caller controls the label — even if it's complex:
<Button onClick={handleSave}>
  <SaveIcon />
  Save changes
</Button>

Vex: "Notice how Button doesn't know about SaveIcon. It just renders its children. This is why composition scales — each component stays simple and focused, but together they assemble into anything."

storyBeats.text: Vex assembles a display on the workbench — a picture frame. Inside it, she places different images, one after another. The frame stays the same; only its contents change.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: A layout component is a frame. It doesn't care what's inside — it just provides the structure. The caller decides the contents. That separation is the key: layout components stay stable, pages stay flexible.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <Panel> layout component that accepts three props: header (JSX), children (main content), and footer (JSX).

  • Render a <div data-testid="panel"> wrapping three elements
  • <div data-testid="panel-header"> — renders the header prop
  • <div data-testid="panel-body"> — renders children
  • <div data-testid="panel-footer"> — renders the footer prop (if provided — it's optional)
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <Modal> component from scratch. It accepts: title (string), children, onClose (callback), and isOpen (boolean). When isOpen is false, render nothing. When true, render an overlay with a centred dialog: the title at the top, a close button, and children as the body. The close button calls onClose.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain composition in React to a developer who relies heavily on configuration props. Why does `<Card title="..." icon="..." footer="...">` become hard to maintain compared to `<Card><CardHeader /><CardBody /><CardFooter /></Card>`? What does the open/closed principle mean in a React context?

options: The JSX content nested between a component's opening and closing tags
An array of all registered child components in the application
The DOM children of the component's root HTML element
Props passed from a child component up to its parent
questions.answer: The JSX content nested between a component's opening and closing tags
questions.explanation:
children is whatever JSX appears between the component's opening and closing tags.

Title

 passes the

JSX as Card's children prop. The Card component renders it with {children}.

questions.prompt: You need a layout with a persistent header and footer, where each page fills the middle. Which approach is correct?
options: A PageLayout component that renders `children` between a header and footer, wrapped around each page component
Copy the header and footer JSX into every page component
Use a `content` prop on each page component to inject the header/footer from outside
Create a global CSS file that adds header/footer via pseudo-elements
questions.answer: A PageLayout component that renders `children` between a header and footer, wrapped around each page component
questions.explanation: A layout wrapper that renders children between persistent header/footer elements is the canonical React pattern. Each page is passed as children — the layout doesn't know what each page contains. Copying the header/footer into every page creates duplication and maintenance burden.

questions.prompt: When is a `content` prop preferable over `children`?
options: When there are multiple named slots needed (e.g. left panel and right panel separately)
children is always preferable — content props are an antipattern
When the content is a string that never changes
When performance is critical — content props avoid unnecessary re-renders
questions.answer: When there are multiple named slots needed (e.g. left panel and right panel separately)
questions.explanation: children handles one implicit slot well. When a component needs two or more distinct content areas (left/right, header/body/footer as separate JSX), named props like left={...} right={...} are cleaner. Both patterns are valid — children for a single slot, named props for multiple distinct slots.
